title: 22. Interview: Master Interview Bank: Evaluation, Tracing & Monitoring (Part 2)
summary: Interview Q&A for Master Interview Bank: Evaluation, Tracing & Monitoring (part 2 of 2).
objectives: Answer the Master Interview Bank: Evaluation, Tracing & Monitoring interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: 4. Architecture & System Design Questions
sections.body:
**Q1**: Design an evaluation pipeline for a customer support RAG chatbot serving 1M queries/day.
**Outline**:
- **Offline**: golden set of 500+ real queries with gold answers, refreshed monthly; nightly regression on every prompt/model change; faithfulness, context precision, E2E answer correctness; pre-merge gate.
- **Online**: 1% sample of prod traffic -> async LLM-judge scoring faithfulness + answer relevance; rolling 24h dashboards; PSI on query embeddings and answer-length distributions.
- **Feedback**: thumbs-up/down, escalations as labels; weekly join with judge scores to detect judge drift.
- **Tools**: Langfuse for tracing + judge runs; dbt for metric aggregation; Grafana dashboards; PagerDuty for SLO breaches.
- **Tradeoffs**: judge cost (~$0.002/query x 10k sampled = $20/day, acceptable); 1% sample gives ~7k/day, enough for PSI; golden-set staleness vs maintenance burden.

**Q2**: How would you set up monitoring for a multi-agent research system?
**Outline**:
- **Per-agent metrics**: success rate, latency, token cost, reflection trigger rate, tool call accuracy.
- **System metrics**: convergence rounds, communication overhead (redundant message rate), total cost-per-task, E2E success.
- **Emergence metrics**: pairwise message similarity over rounds (echo chamber detection), role adherence, information-flow completeness.
- **Tracing**: one trace per request with one span per agent turn and per tool call; attributes include agent role, message round, tool name, tool args.
- **Alerts**: page on cost > 3x baseline or task success < 60% sustained 1h; ticket on convergence rounds trending up or echo-chamber index > threshold.
- **Tradeoffs**: tracing overhead (cap message body length, sample); composite-metric alerts are noisy, prefer per-agent then drill down.

**Q3**: Design a golden dataset for an agentic coding assistant.
**Outline**:
- **Source**: 30% real internal tickets (anonymized), 30% public GitHub issues with merged PRs, 20% adversarial (multi-file, cross-service, vague), 20% regression cases from past bugs.
- **Size**: 300 for development regression; 1000 for benchmarking.
- **Labels per item**: ticket text, repo state (commit hash), gold patch (or acceptance test), acceptable alternatives, expected trajectory (loose — multiple valid paths), difficulty rating.
- **Scoring**: E2E (patch passes tests?), TAC (args correct?), trajectory efficiency (steps vs gold), side-effect score (modified files outside scope?).
- **Refresh**: monthly from new tickets; quarterly adversarial additions.
- **Tradeoffs**: gold patches lock in one solution — alternatives required; trajectory labels are loose because many paths are valid.

**Q4**: Architect a tracing system for an MCP-based agent using 5 tool servers.
**Outline**:
- **Instrumentation**: OTel SDK in the agent; each MCP server emits spans via OTel exporter; trace context propagated through MCP request headers.
- **Span structure**: root span = user request; child spans = agent turns; grandchildren = tool calls (one per server); attributes: server name, tool name, args (redacted), result summary, status.
- **Backend**: Langfuse (self-hosted) for cost control; 30-day raw retention, 1-year aggregated metrics.
- **Sampling**: tail-based — 100% errors, 100% slow (p95+), 5% healthy, 100% of high-stakes tasks.
- **PII**: redaction layer at instrumentation time; field-level encryption for free-text args.
- **Tradeoffs**: cross-server trace propagation requires OTel headers in MCP — may need protocol extension; per-server circuit breakers must log to traces so failures are visible.

**Q5**: How would you evaluate a multi-modal agent (text + vision)?
**Outline**:
- **Tasks**: image-grounded QA, image editing, chart interpretation, screenshot-driven UI automation.
- **Metrics**: task success, grounding accuracy (does the agent reference the right region?), faithfulness (answer supported by image content?), trajectory efficiency.
- **Judge**: multimodal LLM judge (GPT-4V-class) with vision rubric; human spot-check on 5% sample.
- **Golden set**: 200+ items with image, query, gold answer, gold grounding (bounding boxes or region descriptions).
- **Failure modes**: hallucinated image content, ignored visual cues, OCR errors compounding, region-localization drift.
- **Tradeoffs**: multimodal judges are expensive and biased; ground-truth bounding boxes are expensive to label — consider weak labels from VLM cross-checks.

**Q6**: Design a CI/CD pipeline that gates deploys on evaluation results.
**Outline**:
- **Pre-merge**: developer runs 50-item smoke golden set locally; PR check runs 200-item regression set; must not regress any metric by > 2 points.
- **Pre-deploy**: full 500-item golden set + 100 adversarial items; faithfulness, E2E success, safety metrics; must pass SLOs.
- **Canary**: 5% traffic for 24h; compare to baseline on judge scores, latency, cost, error rate; auto-rollback on regression.
- **Post-deploy**: 7-day watch with sampled prod evaluation; weekly review of sliced metrics.
- **Tools**: Langfuse eval API, GitHub Actions, canary via feature flag, Grafana dashboards.
- **Tradeoffs**: pre-merge latency (regression set takes 10 min — cache results); canary false positives (set thresholds based on historical variance).

**Q7**: How would you build a continuous-eval loop that feeds production failures back into the golden set?
**Outline**:
- **Capture**: every thumbs-down, escalation, retried query logged with full trace.
- **Triage**: weekly review; human labels each as true failure with category, user error, or edge case.
- **Promotion**: true failures -> golden set with gold answer; edge cases -> adversarial set.
- **Sampling**: 5% of unrated prod traffic also reviewed to fight selection bias.
- **Versioning**: golden set versioned; model re-evaluated; regressions flagged.
- **Tradeoffs**: feedback volume can overwhelm triage; deduplicate by query clustering; bias toward high-stakes failures.

**Q8**: Design an LLM-judge pipeline that scales to 10M evaluations/month.
**Outline**:
- **Model selection**: cheap judge (Haiku-class) for triage, expensive (Sonnet/Opus) for borderline and high-stakes.
- **Caching**: cache by (input hash, judge version) — many queries are similar.
- **Batching**: batch judge calls; async queue with priority lanes.
- **Sampling**: judge 100% of high-stakes, 10% of normal, 1% of low-stakes.
- **Calibration**: rolling 200-item meta-eval set; alert if judge-human kappa drops.
- **Cost**: at $0.001 per cheap call, 10M x 5% sampled x cheap = ~$500/month; add $5k for expensive-tier on borderline.
- **Tradeoffs**: cheap judges have higher error — ensemble with 2 cheap judges for borderline cases; cache hit rate drops as prompts diversify.

**Q9**: Architect a feedback-collection system that minimizes selection bias.
**Outline**:
- **Implicit signals**: retries, escalations, time-on-page, copy-button clicks, follow-up clarifications — captured passively for every user.
- **Explicit signals**: thumbs, star ratings, free-text feedback — only from engaged users (biased).
- **Active sampling**: prompt 5% of users for feedback at random, not just after a bad experience.
- **Weighting**: weight explicit feedback by user segment to correct over-representation.
- **Unrated sampling**: randomly sample 5% of unrated outputs for human review — your unbiased signal.
- **Tools**: event pipeline (Kafka), labeling queue, weighted aggregation in metric dashboards.
- **Tradeoffs**: random feedback prompts annoy users — cap at 1 per user per week; human review is expensive — cap at 5%.

**Q10**: Design a tracing system that survives a 10x traffic spike without exploding costs.
**Outline**:
- **Adaptive sampling**: head-based at 1% baseline, dynamically downshift to 0.1% during spikes (preserve error traces via tail-based layer).
- **Tiered storage**: hot tier (7 days, full fidelity) -> warm (30 days, sampled) -> cold (1 year, aggregated metrics only).
- **Attribute minimization**: drop prompt/completion text during spikes, keep only token counts and hashes.
- **Async export**: decouple span emission from request path; buffer to local queue, batch-export.
- **Budget caps**: hard cap on daily trace volume; over-budget -> drop to error-only sampling.
- **Tradeoffs**: during spikes debugging fidelity drops — pre-define which traces to preserve (errors, p99 latency, high-cost) so the cap doesn't kill signal.

sections.title: 5. Rapid-Fire Definitions
sections.body:
**BLEU** — Precision-based n-gram overlap metric with brevity penalty; designed for translation.
**ROUGE** — Recall-oriented n-gram overlap metric; standard for summarization.
**BERTScore** — Embedding-based semantic similarity using token-level cosine similarity.
**Perplexity** — Exponentiated average negative log-likelihood; lower = more confident on test text.
**MMLU** — Massive Multitask Language Understanding; 57-subject multiple-choice benchmark.
**HumanEval** — 164 hand-written Python programming problems for code generation.
**GSM8K** — Grade-school math word problems benchmark for multi-step reasoning.
**SWE-bench** — Software-engineering benchmark of GitHub issues with merged PRs.
**Contamination** — Eval data appearing in training data, inflating scores.
**LLM-as-a-Judge** — Using an LLM to score outputs against a rubric.
**Pointwise judge** — Scores one output on an absolute scale.
**Pairwise judge** — Compares two outputs, picks the better one.
**Position bias** — Judge prefers first or second output regardless of quality.
**Verbosity bias** — Judge prefers longer outputs.
**Self-preference** — Judge prefers outputs from its own model family.
**RAGAS** — RAG Assessment framework with faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision/recall.
**Faithfulness** — Fraction of answer claims supported by retrieved context.
**Context precision** — Fraction of retrieved chunks relevant to the query.
**Context recall** — Fraction of needed information successfully retrieved.
**Graph RAG** — Retrieval over an entity-relationship graph for multi-hop reasoning.
**Agentic RAG** — Agent iteratively calls retrieval as a tool with planning and self-correction.
**Self-RAG** — Model emits reflection tokens to decide when to retrieve and whether answers are supported.
**CRAG** — Corrective RAG; scores retrieved chunks and falls back to web search if confidence is low.
**Task success rate (TSR/ESR)** — Fraction of tasks where the agent achieves the goal.
**Trajectory efficiency** — Steps taken vs optimal steps.
**TSA** — Tool Selection Accuracy.
**TAC** — Tool Argument Correctness.
**Span** — Single unit of work in a trace with timing, attributes, and status.
**Trace** — Tree of spans representing one request.
**OpenTelemetry (OTel)** — Vendor-neutral spec for spans, traces, metrics, logs.
**OpenLLMetry / OpenInference** — OTel semantic conventions for LLM/AI spans.
**Head-based sampling** — Decision at span creation; cheap, misses rare failures.
**Tail-based sampling** — Decision after trace completes; allows "keep all errors" rules.
**LangSmith** — LangChain's commercial tracing + eval platform.
**Langfuse** — Open-source, framework-agnostic tracing + eval platform.
**Data drift** — Input distribution changes.
**Concept drift** — Input-to-output relationship changes.
**Prediction drift** — Output distribution changes.
**Upstream drift** — Dependency (retrieval index, LLM version) changes silently.
**PSI** — Population Stability Index; <0.1 stable, >0.25 significant drift.
**Golden dataset** — Curated, labeled set used as a regression baseline.
**Inter-annotator agreement (IAA)** — How often raters agree; reported as Cohen's or Fleiss' kappa.
**Dataset leakage** — Golden items appearing in training data, inflating scores.
**MCP (Model Context Protocol)** — Open protocol for tool/resource/prompt discovery and calling.
**Function calling** — Model-level capability to emit JSON args per a provided schema.
**Side effect** — Unintended state change caused by an agent action.
**Oversight-trigger rate** — Fraction of runs where the agent escalates to a human.
**Echo chamber** — Multi-agent failure where agents reinforce a wrong answer without disagreement.
**Credit assignment** — Attributing multi-agent success/failure to individual agents.

sections.title: 6. Cheat Sheet Tables
sections.body:
### Table A: Metric → When To Use

| Metric | Use When | Avoid When |
|--------|----------|-----------|
| BLEU | Translation, template extraction, exact-match needed | Open-ended generation, paraphrasing |
| ROUGE-L | Summarization with ordering sensitivity | Semantic equivalence matters |
| BERTScore | Paraphrase-friendly semantic similarity | Factual correctness against sources |
| Perplexity | Pretraining sanity checks, model comparison on same data | Product quality, downstream task performance |
| Exact match (EM) | Short factual QA, single correct answer | Summarization, open-ended QA |
| F1 (token) | Extractive QA with partial credit | Semantic equivalence |
| LLM-judge pointwise | Cheap scaling, rubric-based scoring | High-stakes without human review |
| LLM-judge pairwise | Ranking models, A/B decisions | Need absolute scores per item |
| Faithfulness (RAGAS) | RAG hallucination detection | Non-RAG generation |
| Context precision | Diagnosing over-retrieval | No retrieval system |
| Context recall | Diagnosing under-retrieval | No retrieval system |
| TSA | Agent tool selection debugging | Agents with no tools |
| TAC | Argument correctness debugging | Same as above |
| Trajectory efficiency | Cost/latency optimization | Single-shot outputs |
| PSI | Drift detection on any distribution | Categorical rare events (use chi-square) |
| Cohen's kappa | Annotator agreement | Single annotator |

### Table B: Tool → Best For

| Tool | Best For | Watch Out For |
|------|----------|---------------|
| LangSmith | LangChain/LangGraph shops wanting polish | Vendor lock-in, cost at scale |
| Langfuse | Self-hosting, multi-framework, cost control | Less hand-holding than LangSmith |
| OpenTelemetry | Vendor-neutral standard instrumentation | Lower-level; needs semantic conventions |
| OpenLLMetry | Plug-and-play OTel for LLMs | Limited to supported frameworks |
| Arize Phoenix | ML/AI observability with eval suite | General-purpose; less RAG-specific |
| Braintrust | Eval-first platform with prompt playground | Newer ecosystem |
| Promptfoo | CLI-driven eval, prompt testing | Not a tracing backend |
| Ragas (library) | RAG-specific metrics in Python | Requires careful judge calibration |
| DeepEval | Unit-test-style eval assertions | Pydantic-heavy; API churn |
| Datadog / Honeycomb | Generic observability, APM roots | Less AI-specific semantics |
| Garak / PurpleLlama | Red-teaming and safety eval | Safety-only, not general quality |

### Table C: Failure Mode → Likely Cause

| Symptom | Likely Root Cause | First Debug Step |
|---------|-------------------|------------------|
| BLEU up, users complain | Metric gaming; template-y outputs | Spot-check 20 outputs blind |
| Faithfulness dropped, no code change | Silent LLM update or index rebuild | Check provider changelog, index diff |
| Cost doubled overnight | Token inflation, retries, routing change | Compare token distributions day-over-day |
| Golden set 100%, users unhappy | Staleness or leakage | Sample prod traffic, compare to golden |
| Metrics fine, complaints spike | Segment failure hidden by averages | Slice metrics by segment and time |
| TSA 95%, ESR 60% | Wrong args, wrong order, ignored results | Compute TAC; pull failing traces |
| CRAG triggers 80% | Weak primary retrieval | Score context precision directly |
| Two agents keep agreeing | Echo chamber / sycophancy | Measure pairwise message similarity |
| p95 latency 8s, p50 1s | Long-tail: loops, slow tools, cold starts | Pull 20 p95 traces and categorize |
| Multi-agent 8x slower | Coordination overhead, redundant messages | Measure communication overhead |
| Agent succeeds but takes 15 steps | Loops, over-reflection, redundant verification | Detect loops; review reflection triggers |
| Graph RAG fails multi-hop | Traversal logic or graph coverage gap | Walk gold path manually; compare |
| MCP server crash mid-task | No circuit breaker, no fallback | Chaos test; add timeout + fallback |
| Debate doesn't converge | Stable disagreement cycle | Cap rounds; add judge agent |
| Agent hallucinates 1% | Distributed; check for clusters | Pull 100 traces; cluster by feature |
| Trace storage $5k/mo | No sampling, verbose attributes, no TTL | Tail-sample, drop prompt text, set TTL |

sections.title: 7. Interview Strategy Tips
sections.body:
### Structuring Your Answer

For conceptual questions, use **definition → tradeoff → example**: one sentence on what it is, one on when it works/doesn't, one concrete case. For scenario questions, use **STAR-E**: Situation (restate), Task (what's being asked), Action (your debugging moves in order), Result (what you'd expect to find), Edge cases (what could go wrong with your approach). For design questions, use **components → metrics → tradeoffs**: name the parts, the metrics each needs, then the explicit tradeoffs you'd surface to the interviewer.

### Common Mistakes Candidates Make

- **Jumping to a solution without diagnosing.** Always state what you'd measure first, then what you'd change. Interviewers want structured debugging, not lucky guesses.
- **Naming metrics without explaining tradeoffs.** "I'd use BLEU" without saying "because exact-match is the priority" or "I'd avoid BLEU because outputs are paraphrased" is a missed signal.
- **Treating LLM-judge as ground truth.** Senior candidates always mention judge calibration, biases, and the need for human spot-checks.
- **Ignoring cost.** Every architecture answer should address cost. "Sample 100% of traffic" is almost always wrong at scale.
- **Forgetting safety and PII.** In agent and tracing questions, raise redaction, side effects, and oversight unprompted — it shows seniority.
- **No questions for the interviewer.** Always have 2–3 thoughtful questions ready (see below).

### What Interviewers Are Really Testing

- **Structured thinking** — can you decompose a vague problem into measurable sub-questions?
- **Tradeoff awareness** — do you understand that every metric and tool has costs, not just benefits?
- **Production realism** — do you think about scale, cost, drift, failure modes, not just paper results?
- **Honesty about limits** — can you say "this metric is wrong for this task" instead of cargo-culting?
- **Curiosity** — do you ask sharp follow-up questions, or just answer what's asked?

### How To Admit You Don't Know

Say "I haven't worked with X directly, but here's how I'd approach it: ..." then reason from first principles. Interviewers respect honest unknowns paired with structured reasoning. Avoid bluffing — follow-up questions will expose it, and the bluff itself is a red flag. If truly stuck, ask a clarifying question: "Are you asking about the protocol itself or its production usage?" That buys time and shows engagement.

### Questions You Should Ask The Interviewer

- "What does your eval pipeline look like today? Golden set size, judge model, refresh cadence?"
- "How do you handle drift detection — PSI, manual review, or something else?"
- "What's your tracing backend, and what's your sampling strategy?"
- "What's the most surprising failure mode you've hit in production?"
- "How do you balance shipping speed against eval rigor — who owns the gate?"
- "What does the on-call experience look like for the AI system — what wakes people up?"
- "How do you measure the cost of an agent run, and who pays for it — product, infra, or shared?"

These signal that you think about eval, tracing, monitoring, and operations as a connected system — not just model quality in isolation. They also give you real signal about whether the team is mature or firefighting.

**End of file 11.** You now have the consolidated interview bank. Use Section 2 for conceptual fluency, Section 3 for scenario practice, Section 4 for system-design framing, Section 5 for night-before review, Section 6 for fast lookup, and Section 7 for delivery. Good luck.
